content: When a pesticide product is associated with more than one Globally Harmonized System (GHS) health hazard, specific rules govern the precedence of symbols and signal words displayed on the label: 1. If the skull-and-crossbones symbol is required for one hazard, the exclamation mark symbol for another hazard should not be included. 2. If the corrosive symbol is required, the exclamation mark symbol should not be used for skin or eye irritation. 3. If the health hazard symbol is used for respiratory sensitization, the exclamation mark should not appear for skin sensitization or skin/eye irritation. All assigned hazard statements must be included on the label, except in cases where the statement H314 (causes severe skin burns and eye damage) is assigned. In such cases, the statement H318 (causes serious eye damage) may be omitted. If hazard color bands are displayed on the label and the pesticide product has multiple GHS health hazards, only the most hazardous color band should be shown. Health Hazards and Labeling Relevance Germ Cell Mutagenicity: Pesticides with this classification are unlikely to be authorized in most countries. If authorized, appropriate hazard labeling is required. Carcinogenicity: Similarly, carcinogenic pesticides are rarely authorized. If they are, proper labeling must be implemented. Reproductive Toxicity: Pesticides classified as reproductive toxicants are also unlikely to be authorized. If authorized, they must be labeled accordingly. Pesticides causing chronic organ toxicity are generally not authorized. If authorized, they require proper labeling. Aspiration Hazard: This hazard is likely to be indicated on pesticide labels. It is not recommended to mix GHS classification with the World Health Organization (WHO) classification for pesticide labeling. For example, the WHO classification for acute toxicity should not be combined with GHS classifications for other health hazards. To avoid conflicts and user confusion, countries should apply either the GHS or WHO classification consistently for all health hazards. Transition from WHO to GHS The GHS is increasingly adopted globally for chemical classification and labeling. Harmonized classification improves understanding of chemical risks and facilitates international trade. The FAO and WHO recommend the progressive adoption of the GHS for pesticide classification and labeling. However, many countries still use the WHO classification. Countries transitioning from WHO to GHS should do so on a fixed date and for all pesticide labels simultaneously, providing sufficient notice to manufacturers and distributors to prepare new labels and logistics. Environmental Hazards Currently, the GHS classifies only aquatic environmental hazards and ozone layer hazards. For labeling purposes, the pesticide formulation or end-user product should be classified, not just the active ingredient. If a product poses multiple GHS environmental hazards, precedence rules apply: If H410 (very toxic to aquatic life with long-lasting effects) is assigned, H400 (very toxic to aquatic life) may be omitted. If H411 (toxic to aquatic life with long-lasting effects) is assigned, H401 (toxic to aquatic life) may be omitted. If H412 (harmful to aquatic life with long-lasting effects) is assigned, H402 (harmful to aquatic life) may be omitted. Environmental risk assessments may also result in specific precautionary statements and pictograms on the label, addressing a broader range of risks, such as effects on birds, wildlife, livestock, bees, soil organisms, and groundwater. Information, Training, and Compliance Pesticide labels are essential tools for providing information on safe and effective use. This is especially true for users who are illiterate, cannot read the label language, or face cultural barriers in understanding pictograms. Therefore, risk communication strategies should extend beyond labels, using media, posters, billboards, and other accessible formats. Governments and the pesticide industry should establish systems to regularly inform and train users on proper pesticide use, risks, and label interpretation. This is particularly important when new label elements, such as pictograms, are introduced. A more sustainable approach would be to include pesticide label education in school curricula. Inspectors should report label-related issues to improve their effectiveness.
